clue.text: Feminist writer reversed time line in ludicrous comedy fast, presumably

indicators.note: the clue says the whole string built from the following pieces is written backwards

parts.note: a farce is a comedy built on absurd situations

indicators.note: in tells us the line letter goes inside the 'not slow' phrase

parts.note: something fast is presumably not slow, so the phrase gives NOT SLOW

explanation.surface: A feminist author's daring flip of a timeline inside an absurd, quick-fire comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fast, presumably' is a whimsical definition by opposite; 'reversed' then turns the entire assembled string round, not just one piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Mary Wollstonecraft wrote A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792), a founding text of feminism.

clue.text: More suitable to get dismissed over Top Gear producer

indicators.note: in a down clue, over places the dismissal word above the other piece

parts.note: a batsman who is dismissed is out
fitter is the comparative of fit, meaning more suitable

explanation.surface: A fitter presenter is dismissed from the motoring show Top Gear and the producer takes over.
explanation.walkthrough: Top Gear is a British TV motoring show; here 'Top' and 'Gear' are clothing, as in tops and outfits.
explanation.definitionFit: A firm that supplies clothing and equipment provides tops and other gear to customers.

clue.text: Air bag reduced sudden forward movement

indicators.note: reduced means the word is cut short by losing its final letter

parts.note: a lunge is a sudden thrust forward

explanation.surface: A car's airbag inflates less during a sudden jolt forward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Air bag' suggests a car safety device, but it describes a breathing organ.
explanation.definitionFit: A breathing organ is literally a bag that fills with air.

clue.text: Peevish about artist, against misrepresentation

indicators.note: about means the peevish word goes around the other letters

parts.note: peevish and testy both mean irritable
RA is a Royal Academician, a crossword artist
V is short for versus, meaning against

explanation.surface: A grumpy critic attacks an artist, objecting to a distorted portrayal.
explanation.walkthrough: RA, a Royal Academician, is the crossword's standard artist; 'against' as V comes from versus.
explanation.definitionFit: A travesty is a grotesque distortion or mockery of something, a gross misrepresentation.

clue.text: Tell end of story, unless starting?

indicators.note: starting tells us the negative word moves to the start of the phrase

parts.note: unless means if not

indicators.note: end of picks the final letter of story

explanation.surface: Someone is asked to reveal how a story finishes, unless it has not begun yet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starting' moves NOT to the front of IF NOT, giving NOTIF, and the Y from 'end of story' follows.
explanation.definitionFit: To inform someone formally is to tell them something.

clue.text: During endless selection, special school dismisses head who may be addicted to bars

definitions.text: who may be addicted to bars

indicators.note: During means one piece sits inside the other
endless means the word loses its last letter

parts.note: a choice is a selection

indicators.note: special signals the remaining letters are rearranged
dismisses head means the first letter of school is removed

explanation.surface: A special school expels its headteacher partway through a selection process.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endless' gives CHOIC; 'dismisses head' leaves CHOOL, which 'special' rearranges to COHOL; 'During' puts that inside CHOIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Bars here are chocolate bars, so this is someone hooked on chocolate.

clue.text: Central Scottish location of more than half of wartime sitcom

indicators.note: more than half of means only the first five of eight letters are kept

parts.note: 'Allo 'Allo! was a BBC sitcom set in occupied France in the Second World War

explanation.surface: A Scottish town hosts more than half of a wartime sitcom's filming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Allo 'Allo! is a British TV comedy; its title has eight letters, and keeping five gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Alloa is a town in Clackmannanshire, in the Central Belt of Scotland.

clue.text: Nobody special from male cast of Neighbours?

definitions.meaning: an ordinary, unremarkable young man, the familiar type everyone knows
a young man living in the adjacent house; Neighbours is a long-running Australian TV soap

explanation.surface: The men in the soap Neighbours are all ordinary nobodies.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes a wholesome, ordinary young man, and literally the lad living next to you.

clue.text: Melting ice cap and atoll I am relating to planet's past conditions

indicators.note: melting suggests the letters losing shape and re-forming in a new order

explanation.surface: An atoll dweller warns of the melting polar ice cap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Melting' rearranges ICE CAP and ATOLL I AM; 'and' joins the two parts of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Palaeoclimatology studies Earth's climate in the geological past, so this adjective describes ancient climates.

clue.text: Tango inscribed in bizarre annotated scratching over page?

indicators.note: inscribed in means one letter is written inside the others
bizarre signals the letters are jumbled
scratching means crossing out a letter

parts.note: O is the cricket scoring abbreviation for an over
Tango is T in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone scrawls a dance note into a strangely annotated sheet, scratching over the page.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scratching' removes O from ANNOTATED, 'bizarre' jumbles ANNTATED, and 'inscribed in' adds T inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A page is a young servant or helper who waits on someone, as at a wedding.

clue.text: Hardy familiarly abridged archaic fiction

indicators.note: abridged means shortened by dropping the final letter

parts.note: something archaic is old
a fiction is a lie

explanation.surface: Thomas Hardy's antique novels in shortened editions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hardy' suggests the novelist, but it is Oliver Hardy of Laurel and Hardy.
explanation.definitionFit: The pet form of Oliver, as Stan Laurel's comedy partner Oliver Hardy was known.

clue.text: Briefly straighten out satirical character

indicators.note: briefly means cut short by losing the final letter

parts.note: to align is to straighten or put in line

explanation.surface: A satirist is asked to quickly straighten out a character.
explanation.definitionFit: Ali G is the spoof interviewer created by comedian Sacha Baron Cohen.

clue.text: Complain excessively about dull, large fruit

parts.note: to beef is slang for to complain

indicators.note: about means the word for excessively goes around the dull word

parts.note: too means excessively
mat is a variant of matt, meaning dull, not shiny

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles too much about a boring, oversized fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beef' is informal for a grievance or to grumble; 'dull' wants to be part of the definition but is the inserted piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A beef tomato is an especially big, fleshy variety of tomato.

clue.text: Lifted lid on whether island villain supplies countries around ocean

indicators.note: in a down clue, on puts the first piece above the rest
in a down clue, lifted means the word is read upwards, so backwards

parts.note: a cap is a lid
if can mean whether, as in 'ask if'
crim is informal for a criminal

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a villain on an island lifted the lid on a supply racket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lifted' turns CAP up the column to give PAC.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pacific Rim is the group of nations bordering the Pacific Ocean.

clue.text: Open University discrimination involving Conservative social reject

indicators.note: involving means the discrimination word wraps around the letter

parts.note: taste is discernment, the ability to discriminate

explanation.surface: A distance-learning university's prejudice against a Tory creates a social pariah.
explanation.walkthrough: 'discrimination' suggests prejudice but means good judgement; 'involving' puts C inside TASTE as T-C-ASTE.
explanation.definitionFit: An outcaste is a person cast out of their caste or society, a social outsider.

clue.text: Possible part of a Chinese request for delay that's rebuffed?

indicators.note: rebuffed suggests being pushed back, so the phrase is read backwards

parts.note: 'not now' asks someone to put something off

explanation.surface: A Chinese person's plea to postpone is turned down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a Chinese' means a Chinese takeaway meal, an everyday British usage.
explanation.definitionFit: A dumpling commonly served in soup or fried as part of a Chinese meal.

clue.text: Reserves arrived breezily on English sommelier's recommendation, say

parts.note: TA, the Territorial Army, was Britain's volunteer reserve force
to blow in is to arrive casually

explanation.surface: Reserve soldiers drop in casually and accept the wine waiter's suggestion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' is a link here: in a down clue the pieces simply run in order.
explanation.definitionFit: Ordinary wine drunk with a meal is an example of what a wine waiter might suggest.

clue.text: Very exciting men chat with Mike

parts.note: OR, other ranks, are soldiers who are not officers
to gas is to chatter idly
mike or mic is short for microphone

explanation.surface: Soldiers gossip with someone called Mike, and it is thrilling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mike' looks like a name but is a microphone.
explanation.definitionFit: Used loosely, the word describes something intensely thrilling or pleasurable.

clue.text: Poet doing play in need of an ending

indicators.note: in need of an ending means the word's last letter is missing

parts.note: larking about is playing around

explanation.surface: A poet working on a play still lacks a final scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'doing play' suggests staging drama, but means fooling around.
explanation.definitionFit: Philip Larkin was an English poet, author of The Whitsun Weddings.

clue.text: Black, gay emblem cropped by someone bright

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils

indicators.note: cropped means the last letter is cut off

parts.note: the rainbow flag is the emblem of gay pride
X means by, as in measurements like 3 x 4

explanation.surface: A pride emblem in black is trimmed by a clever person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by' looks like a link word, but it gives X.
explanation.definitionFit: Brainbox is informal British slang for a highly intelligent person.

clue.text: Skiers churning mush

indicators.note: churning suggests the letters stirred into a new order

explanation.surface: Skiers churn the snow into slush.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mush' suggests slushy snow, but is slang for the face.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are British slang for the face or mouth.

clue.text: I'm facing changes, attending an evensong feature?

indicators.note: changes signals the letters before it are rearranged

parts.note: at means present at, attending

explanation.surface: Someone confronts big changes while going to an evening church service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changes' rearranges I'M FACING; 'an' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The canticle of Mary is sung at evening prayer, so it is a regular part of that service.

clue.text: Tool to apply lubricant coat of grease and slime

parts.note: a grease gun is the tool used to apply lubricant

indicators.note: coat of means the outside letters of the word

explanation.surface: A mechanic's grease gun leaves a coating of oily slime.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for any sticky, messy substance or sludge.

clue.text: Part of garden absorbing a spot of water?

indicators.note: absorbing means the garden word takes the letter inside

parts.note: a flower bed is a part of a garden

explanation.surface: A garden bed soaks up a drop of water.
explanation.definitionFit: A drop of liquid, such as a droplet of sweat, is described as a bead.

clue.text: Chatterer would audibly nag

indicators.note: audibly means the words are said aloud

parts.note: the jay is a noisy, chattering bird, and 'would' contracts to 'd

explanation.surface: A gossip would audibly pester someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nag' suggests pestering, but means a worn-out horse.
explanation.definitionFit: An old word for a tired or worthless horse.

clue.text: Settled course only covered by right back

indicators.note: back means the assembled letters are read in reverse
covered by means the word for only sits inside the abbreviation

parts.note: one can mean only, as in 'my one hope'

explanation.surface: A settled route is protected only by the right-back defender.
explanation.walkthrough: 'right back' looks like a football position; 'back' reverses R-ONE-T.
explanation.definitionFit: The general drift or course of something, as in the even tenor of life.

clue.text: Phone card prepared by one company on the same wavelength?

parts.note: a SIM card goes in a mobile phone
a pat answer is one prepared in advance
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A phone SIM card set up by a firm that shares your frequency.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone congenial and like-minded, sharing your outlook, is a kindred spirit.

clue.text: All in, supplied with cheeseboard accompaniments?

definitions.meaning: exhausted; the phrase is Cockney rhyming slang for knackered, British slang for worn out
provided with biscuits of a plain type served with cheese

explanation.surface: Everyone is included and given the biscuits for the cheese course.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhyming slang for exhausted, which literally reads as being given plain biscuits for cheese.
